entries.meaning: A figure showing the size, length, or amount of something. ---
examples: Take a measurement before you cut the board.
The tailor wrote down all my measurements.
That measurement looks off by half an inch.
entries.contrast: The s is a zh sound, as in pleasure: MEZH-ur-muhnt.

entries.meaning: A unit or standard used to state size or amount. ---
examples: A cup is a standard measure in American recipes.
The inch is an old measure of length.
The rest of the world uses metric measures.

entries.meaning: A fixed amount used as a standard for measuring. ---
examples: The meter is the basic unit of length in the metric system.
Convert both numbers to the same units before you add them.
Electricity is billed by the unit.
entries.contrast: It starts with a y sound, so it takes a, not an: a unit.

entries.meaning: How large or small something is. ---
examples: What size shoe do you wear?
The two rooms are almost the same size.
They carry that shirt in three sizes.

entries.meaning: The measurement of something from one end to the other. ---
examples: Measure the length of the table first.
The pool is fifty meters in length.
Cut two lengths of rope the same size.

entries.meaning: The measurement of something from one side to the other. ---
examples: Check the width of the doorway before you buy the couch.
The hallway is only three feet in width.
The fabric comes in two widths.
entries.contrast: It comes from wide, but the vowel is short: WIDTH.

entries.meaning: How tall something or someone is. ---
examples: The nurse recorded her height and weight.
Adjust the height of the chair.
The shelves come in three different heights.
entries.contrast: Spelled like eight but it rhymes with kite: HYT. There is no th on the end.

entries.meaning: How deep something is from the top down. ---
examples: The lake reaches a depth of sixty feet.
Plant the bulbs at a depth of four inches.
Divers explored the depths of the canyon.

entries.meaning: How thick something is from one surface to the other. ---
examples: Check the thickness of the ice before you walk on it.
The steel plate is half an inch in thickness.
Sand the board until the thickness is even.

entries.meaning: The amount of space between two places or things. ---
examples: What's the distance from here to the airport?
He can throw a football a good distance.
They drove long distances every weekend.

entries.meaning: How heavy something is, or a heavy object used for lifting or holding something down. ---
examples: The scale shows my weight in pounds.
He lifts weights three mornings a week.
Put a weight on the papers so they don't blow away.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like wait; the gh is silent.

entries.meaning: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. ---
examples: An object keeps the same mass on the moon.
Scientists measure mass in kilograms, not pounds.
Mass and weight are not the same thing.

entries.meaning: The amount of space that something fills. ---
examples: Find the volume of the box in cubic inches.
Water expands in volume when it freezes.
The tank holds a large volume of fuel.

entries.meaning: The amount that a container or a space can hold. ---
examples: The tank has a capacity of twenty gallons.
The stadium was filled to capacity.
The two coolers have different capacities.

entries.meaning: The size of a flat surface, found by multiplying length by width. ---
examples: Calculate the area of the floor before you order tile.
The lot has an area of about half an acre.
Add the areas of the two rooms together.

entries.meaning: How fast something moves. ---
examples: Cut your speed on the wet road.
The train reaches speeds of 150 miles an hour.
He read the whole book at record speed.

entries.meaning: Speed in a particular direction, used in science. ---
examples: The rocket reached escape velocity.
They measured the bullet's velocity.
Wind velocities were highest near the coast.

entries.meaning: The speed at which someone walks, runs, or works. ---
examples: She set a fast pace for the rest of us.
He walked at a steady pace.
The runners hit very different paces in the last mile.

entries.meaning: How fast something happens, measured against time or another amount. ---
examples: Water was leaking at a rate of a gallon an hour.
His heart rate dropped once he sat down.
Interest rates went up again.

entries.meaning: A quantity of something, especially of something you cannot count. ---
examples: Add a small amount of salt.
The amount of rain this spring was unusual.
Large amounts of data were lost.
entries.contrast: Use amount with uncountable nouns and number with countable ones: the amount of water, the number of bottles.

entries.meaning: How much of something there is. ---
examples: Enter the quantity you want to order.
They buy flour in large quantities.
The recipe lists the quantity of each ingredient.

entries.meaning: A measurement such as length, width, or height. ---
examples: Give me the dimensions of the room.
The new box has the same dimensions as the old one.
Height is the third dimension.

entries.meaning: How much mass a material has for its size. ---
examples: Lead has a much higher density than aluminum.
Oil floats on water because of its lower density.
The lab measured the density of each sample.

entries.meaning: A push or a pull acting on an object, measured in newtons. ---
examples: The force of the wind snapped the branch.
Two forces act on the box at the same time.
Apply a steady force to the lever.

entries.meaning: An amount stated as a part of a hundred. ---
examples: A high percentage of the class passed.
What percentage of your income goes to rent?
The two percentages don't add up to a hundred.

entries.meaning: One part in a hundred. ---
examples: About twenty percent of the crop was lost.
Only a few percent of applicants get in.
Sales rose ten percent last quarter.
entries.contrast: Americans write it as one word, percent; the British write per cent. The plural is percent, never percents.

entries.meaning: A part of a whole, such as one half or three quarters. ---
examples: Add the two fractions and reduce the answer.
The repair cost a fraction of what I expected.
Only a small fraction of the seeds came up.

entries.meaning: A number written with a point, such as 0.75. ---
examples: Round the decimal to two places.
Turn the fraction into a decimal.
The chart lists everything in decimals.
entries.contrast: Americans write a decimal point where Russian uses a comma: 3.5, not 3,5.

entries.meaning: The result of adding numbers together and dividing by how many there are. ---
examples: The average of the five scores is eighty-two.
Rainfall was above average this month.
Their batting averages were nearly identical.

entries.meaning: The average of a set of numbers. ---
examples: Report the mean along with the range.
The mean and the median are far apart here.
Both means came out close to fifty.
entries.contrast: The same spelling is also the verb to mean and the adjective mean, unkind.

entries.meaning: The middle value in a list of numbers arranged in order. ---
examples: The median tells you more than the average here.
Half the houses sold above the median.
The two medians were identical.
entries.contrast: In American English the same word also names the strip in the middle of a highway.

entries.meaning: A part of a whole, compared with the rest. ---
examples: A large proportion of the budget goes to salaries.
Mix the paint in the right proportion.
The proportions of sand and cement matter a lot.

entries.meaning: How close a measurement is to the true value. ---
examples: The scale loses accuracy when it's cold.
We double-checked the numbers for accuracy.
GPS gives accuracy within a few feet.

entries.meaning: The level of fine detail that a measurement is made to. ---
examples: The part was machined with great precision.
Lab work demands precision.
You don't need that much precision for a garden fence.

entries.meaning: The amount a measurement is allowed to vary from the exact figure. ---
examples: The part is machined to a tolerance of one thousandth of an inch.
That's outside the tolerance on the drawing.
Aerospace parts have very tight tolerances.

entries.meaning: An extra amount allowed beyond what is strictly needed. ---
examples: Leave a margin of error in your estimate.
He won by a margin of two seconds.
The margins on this drawing are too tight.

entries.meaning: One of the equal steps by which something increases. ---
examples: The dial moves in five-degree increments.
Raise the temperature by a small increment.
You can pay it off in monthly increments.

entries.meaning: The adjusting of an instrument so that its readings are correct. ---
examples: The scale is due for calibration.
Calibration takes about ten minutes.
Poor calibration explains the strange readings.

entries.meaning: A figure shown by a measuring instrument. ---
examples: The meter reading was higher than last month.
Take a reading every hour.
Both readings came out the same.

entries.meaning: The amount of a medicine to be taken and how often. ---
examples: Follow the dosage on the label.
The doctor lowered his dosage.
Children's dosages are based on weight.

entries.meaning: A small part taken from something so that it can be tested. ---
examples: The lab tested a water sample from the well.
Take a sample from the middle of the batch.
All three samples came back clean.
entries.contrast: Americans say SAM-puhl with a short a; the British say SAHM-puhl.

entries.meaning: A standard figure that other results are compared against. ---
examples: That test sets the benchmark for the industry.
Our numbers are below the national benchmark.
They ran the same benchmarks on both machines.

entries.meaning: An agreed level or measure that things are judged against. ---
examples: The meter is the international standard of length.
This part doesn't meet the standard.
Safety standards have gotten stricter.

entries.meaning: A number used to measure how well something is doing. ---
examples: Response time is the metric we watch.
Pick one metric and track it all year.
The dashboard shows a dozen metrics.

entries.meaning: The size or strength of something, especially on a scientific scale. ---
examples: The quake had a magnitude of 6.2.
Nobody grasped the magnitude of the problem.
The two stars differ by three magnitudes.
entries.contrast: Americans say MAG-nuh-tood; the British add a y sound, MAG-nuh-tyood.

entries.meaning: How large something is or how far it reaches. ---
examples: Crews are still assessing the extent of the damage.
To some extent the two counts agree.
The full extent of the flooding wasn't clear until morning.

entries.meaning: The greatest amount that is allowed or possible. ---
examples: The speed limit here is thirty-five.
There's a limit to how much that shelf will hold.
Both weight limits were raised last year.

entries.meaning: The weight carried or supported by something. ---
examples: The truck was carrying a full load.
That beam takes the whole load of the roof.
Heavy loads wear out the springs.

entries.meaning: Large size or volume, especially when it makes something hard to handle. ---
examples: The bulk of the shipment is still in the warehouse.
We buy rice in bulk.
The sheer bulk of the machine made it hard to move.

entries.meaning: The total number found by counting. ---
examples: The final count was two hundred people.
Her white blood cell count is low.
The two counts didn't match.

entries.meaning: A running count kept while things are added up. ---
examples: Keep a tally of how many boxes go out.
The final tally came in after midnight.
Their tallies were off by three.

entries.meaning: The amount you get when everything is added together. ---
examples: The total comes to forty-two dollars.
Add up the column and check the total.
The monthly totals are on the last page.

entries.meaning: A figure that is close to the true one but not exact. ---
examples: That number is only an approximation.
Give me a rough approximation of the cost.
Both approximations were within a few percent.

entries.meaning: A value showing what share of a group falls below it. ---
examples: Her score was in the ninetieth percentile.
The baby is in the fiftieth percentile for height.
The chart is divided into percentiles.

entries.meaning: A number, especially one in a report or a set of results. ---
examples: Sales figures come out on Monday.
That figure includes shipping.
Check the figures one more time.
entries.contrast: Americans say FIG-yur; the British say FIG-ur.

entries.meaning: Any one of the symbols from 0 to 9. ---
examples: The code is four digits long.
The last digit was smudged.
Drop the final digit and round up.

entries.meaning: An American unit of length equal to 2.54 centimeters. ---
examples: The board is one inch thick.
We got six inches of snow overnight.
Move it over an inch or two.

entries.meaning: An American unit of distance equal to about 1.6 kilometers. ---
examples: The store is two miles down the road.
She runs a mile every morning.
We drove three hundred miles in one day.

entries.meaning: The basic metric unit of length, equal to about 39 inches. ---
examples: The pool is fifty meters long.
Add another meter of cable.
The two rooms differ by half a meter.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it meter, the British metre. The same American spelling also names a measuring device, as in a gas meter.

entries.meaning: One hundredth of a meter. ---
examples: The cut is about three centimeters long.
Trim one centimeter off each side.
The chart is marked in centimeters.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it centimeter, the British centimetre.

entries.meaning: One thousandth of a meter. ---
examples: The gap is only two millimeters wide.
Drill a hole eight millimeters across.
A dime is about one millimeter thick.

entries.meaning: One thousand meters, a little over six tenths of a mile. ---
examples: The race is ten kilometers long.
The border is a kilometer from here.
Road signs in Canada are in kilometers.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say kih-LAH-muh-tur, with the stress on the second syllable, though KIL-uh-mee-tur is also heard.

entries.meaning: The number of miles a vehicle has traveled, or how far it goes on a gallon of fuel. ---
examples: The car has low mileage for its age.
This truck gets terrible mileage on the highway.
Check the mileage before you buy it.

entries.meaning: A length or an area measured in feet. ---
examples: What's the square footage of the house?
Add up the footage of pipe you'll need.
The listing doesn't give the footage.
entries.русский: метраж, длина или площадь в футах
entries.contrast: The same word also means filmed video material, as in security footage.

entries.meaning: The distance around the outside of a circle. ---
examples: Measure the circumference of the tree trunk.
The Earth's circumference is about 25,000 miles.
The two pipes have different circumferences.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable: sur-KUM-fur-uhns.

entries.meaning: The distance straight across a circle through its center. ---
examples: The pipe is four inches in diameter.
Measure the diameter of the wheel.
Drill bits come in a lot of diameters.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on AM: dy-AM-uh-tur.

entries.meaning: The total distance around the edge of a shape or an area. ---
examples: Walk the perimeter of the lot and measure it.
The fence runs the whole perimeter.
Compare the perimeters of the two fields.

entries.meaning: A unit of water depth equal to six feet. ---
examples: The wreck lies in twenty fathoms of water.
The chart marks the depth in fathoms.
They anchored in six fathoms.
entries.contrast: The th is voiced, as in father: FATH-uhm.

entries.meaning: The distance around something thick, such as a tree or a waist. ---
examples: The oak has a girth of twelve feet.
Airlines limit the length and girth of a bag.
The two trunks had similar girths.

entries.meaning: The distance across something from one side to the other. ---
examples: The field measures a hundred feet in breadth.
The river's breadth surprised us.
They measured the length and breadth of the room.
entries.contrast: It comes from broad, but the vowel is a short e: BREDTH.

entries.meaning: One millionth of a meter, used for very small sizes. ---
examples: The filter traps particles down to five microns.
A human hair is about seventy microns across.
The coating is only a few microns thick.

entries.meaning: An American unit of land area equal to about 4,047 square meters. ---
examples: They farm two hundred acres of corn.
The house sits on half an acre.
He bought forty acres outside town.
entries.contrast: Pronounced AY-kur, with the same first sound as ache.

entries.meaning: An area of land measured in acres. ---
examples: The listing doesn't say how much acreage comes with the house.
They added acreage on the north side.
Most of the acreage is wooded.

entries.meaning: A metric unit of land area equal to 10,000 square meters. ---
examples: The park covers two hundred hectares.
The fire burned thousands of hectares.
One hectare is about two and a half acres.

entries.meaning: A unit of area equal to a square measuring one foot on each side. ---
examples: The apartment is nine hundred square feet.
Tile is sold by the square foot.
Add a hundred square feet for the porch.
entries.contrast: The plural is square feet, never square foots.

entries.meaning: A unit of volume equal to a cube one yard on each side, used for concrete and soil. ---
examples: We need three cubic yards of concrete.
Mulch is sold by the cubic yard.
The dump truck holds ten cubic yards.

entries.meaning: A unit of weight equal to about 28 grams. ---
examples: The letter weighs less than an ounce.
Add four ounces of cheese.
The package came to sixteen ounces.
entries.contrast: Written oz on labels, even though there is no z in the word.

entries.meaning: A unit of weight equal to sixteen ounces, or about 454 grams. ---
examples: I bought two pounds of ground beef.
He lost fifteen pounds over the winter.
The baby weighed seven pounds.
entries.contrast: Abbreviated lb, from Latin. The same word is also the British unit of money.

entries.meaning: An American unit of weight equal to 2,000 pounds. ---
examples: The truck hauls twenty tons of gravel.
That rock must weigh a ton.
They shipped several tons of steel.
entries.contrast: It rhymes with fun. An American ton is 2,000 pounds, not the metric 1,000 kilograms.

entries.meaning: The basic metric unit of weight, about one twenty-eighth of an ounce. ---
examples: Add fifty grams of butter.
The label lists nine grams of sugar.
A paper clip weighs about a gram.
entries.contrast: Americans write gram; the British also spell it gramme.

entries.meaning: A metric unit of weight equal to 1,000 grams, or about 2.2 pounds. ---
examples: The bag holds five kilograms of rice.
He can lift a hundred kilograms.
One kilogram is roughly two pounds.

entries.meaning: One thousandth of a gram, used mostly for medicine. ---
examples: Each tablet contains 200 milligrams.
The doctor cut the dose to fifty milligrams.
Vitamins are measured in milligrams.

entries.meaning: A short, everyday word for a kilogram. ---
examples: The melon weighs about two kilos.
He dropped ten kilos last year.
Buy a kilo of apples.
entries.contrast: Kilo is KEE-loh, but kilogram is KIL-uh-gram.

entries.meaning: A unit showing how much pure gold an alloy contains, out of twenty-four parts. ---
examples: The ring is fourteen karat gold.
Pure gold is twenty-four karats.
Most American wedding bands are eighteen karat or less.
entries.contrast: Karat with a k measures gold purity; carat with a c is the weight of a gemstone. They sound the same.

entries.meaning: One thousandth of a liter. ---
examples: The bottle holds 500 milliliters.
Measure out ten milliliters of syrup.
The syringe is marked in milliliters.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it milliliter, the British millilitre.

entries.meaning: A unit of liquid volume equal to about 30 milliliters. ---
examples: The can holds twelve fluid ounces.
Add two fluid ounces of vanilla.
One fluid ounce is the same as two tablespoons.
entries.contrast: An American fluid ounce is slightly larger than a British one.

entries.meaning: A large unit of dry volume used for grain and produce. ---
examples: Corn was selling at four dollars a bushel.
They picked ten bushels of apples.
The barn held a hundred bushels of wheat.

entries.meaning: The temperature scale used in the United States, on which water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212. ---
examples: It hit ninety degrees Fahrenheit yesterday.
American forecasts are all in Fahrenheit.
Set the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit.

entries.meaning: The temperature scale on which water freezes at zero degrees and boils at 100. ---
examples: Most of the world reports temperatures in Celsius.
Twenty degrees Celsius is a pleasant day.
The recipe gives both Celsius and Fahrenheit.
entries.contrast: Americans say Celsius; the older word centigrade is now rare.

entries.meaning: The scientific unit of temperature, counted up from absolute zero. ---
examples: Water freezes at 273 kelvins.
The bulb's color temperature is 2700 kelvin.
Physicists work in kelvins rather than degrees.

entries.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid turns to vapor. ---
examples: Water reaches its boiling point at 212 degrees Fahrenheit.
Alcohol has a lower boiling point than water.
The two liquids have very different boiling points.

entries.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid turns solid. ---
examples: The freezing point of water is 32 degrees Fahrenheit.
Salt lowers the freezing point of water.
The two solutions have different freezing points.

entries.meaning: The gauge in a vehicle that shows how fast it is going. ---
examples: Keep an eye on the speedometer.
The speedometer only reads up to 120.
Older speedometers were driven by a cable.
entries.contrast: The stress is on DAH, not on speed: spih-DAH-muh-tur.

entries.meaning: The instrument in a vehicle that records the total miles traveled. ---
examples: The odometer just rolled past 100,000.
Check the odometer before you sign anything.
Digital odometers are harder to tamper with.

entries.meaning: A gauge showing how fast an engine is turning. ---
examples: The tachometer jumped when he hit the gas.
Watch the tachometer before you shift.
Some trucks have two tachometers.
entries.contrast: The ch is a hard k: ta-KAH-muh-tur.

entries.meaning: The fastest legal speed on a particular road. ---
examples: The speed limit drops to 25 near the school.
He was ten over the speed limit.
American speed limits are posted in miles per hour.

entries.meaning: An instrument that shows height above sea level. ---
examples: The pilot reset the altimeter before landing.
My watch has a built-in altimeter.
Both altimeters read the same.
entries.contrast: The stress is on TIM: al-TIM-uh-tur.

entries.meaning: A precision tool that measures very small thicknesses and diameters. ---
examples: He checked the shaft with a micrometer.
A micrometer reads down to a thousandth of an inch.
The shop keeps three micrometers in the drawer.
entries.contrast: The tool is my-KRAH-muh-tur; the millionth of a meter is MY-kroh-mee-tur.

entries.meaning: A tool with two adjustable arms for measuring thickness or diameter. ---
examples: Measure the bolt with a caliper.
Digital calipers are cheap now.
He set the calipers to half an inch.
entries.contrast: Usually used in the plural: a pair of calipers. The British spell it calliper.

entries.meaning: A flat half-circle marked in degrees, used for measuring angles. ---
examples: Use a protractor to draw a 45-degree angle.
Every student needs a ruler and a protractor.
The protractors were still in the box.

entries.meaning: An instrument with a magnetic needle that shows direction. ---
examples: Take a compass if you're hiking off trail.
The compass needle swung north.
Both compasses pointed the same way.
entries.contrast: The first syllable is KUM, not KOM. The same word also names the drawing tool for circles.

entries.meaning: A flat stick one yard long, marked off in inches. ---
examples: Measure the curtain with a yardstick.
There's a yardstick behind the door.
Hardware stores used to give away yardsticks.
entries.русский: линейка длиной в ярд (91 см); мерило

entries.meaning: A thin metal rod used to check the level of oil in an engine. ---
examples: Pull the dipstick and wipe it clean.
The oil was below the line on the dipstick.
Some new cars don't have dipsticks at all.

entries.meaning: A handheld instrument that measures voltage, current, and resistance. ---
examples: Test the outlet with a multimeter.
A basic multimeter costs about twenty dollars.
Both multimeters gave the same reading.

entries.meaning: An instrument that measures voltage. ---
examples: Hook the voltmeter up to the battery terminals.
The voltmeter showed only nine volts.
Older voltmeters had a moving needle.

entries.meaning: An instrument that measures wind speed. ---
examples: The anemometer on the roof spun all night.
An anemometer recorded gusts of sixty miles an hour.
The weather station has two anemometers.

entries.meaning: An instrument that measures humidity. ---
examples: The hygrometer in the basement reads 65 percent.
A cheap hygrometer is good enough for a greenhouse.
Both hygrometers agreed within a point or two.

entries.meaning: An instrument that records the shaking of the ground during an earthquake. ---
examples: The seismograph picked up the tremor at three in the morning.
Every seismograph in the state registered the quake.
The lab has a row of seismographs along one wall.
entries.contrast: The first syllable sounds like size: SYZ-muh-graf.

entries.meaning: An open container marked with a scale for measuring rainfall. ---
examples: There was two inches of water in the rain gauge.
He empties the rain gauge every morning.
Volunteers read rain gauges all over the county.
entries.contrast: Gauge is spelled g-a-u-g-e but pronounced GAYJ.

entries.meaning: Equipment that finds the position and speed of objects using radio waves. ---
examples: A trooper caught him on radar doing eighty.
The storm showed up clearly on radar.
Airport radars track every flight.

entries.meaning: A device that detects and measures something such as heat, light, or motion. ---
examples: A sensor turns the porch light on at dusk.
The oxygen sensor needs replacing.
A new car is full of sensors.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like censor, someone who removes content.

entries.meaning: The figures shown on the display of an instrument. ---
examples: The digital readout jumped to 98.6.
Take a photo of the readout.
Both readouts went blank at once.

entries.meaning: A cup marked with a scale for measuring ingredients. ---
examples: Pour the milk into a measuring cup.
A glass measuring cup is easier to read.
Most kitchens have two or three measuring cups.

entries.meaning: A straight-sided glass container marked with a scale, used in laboratories. ---
examples: Pour the solution into a clean beaker.
The beaker is marked in milliliters.
A row of beakers sat on the lab bench.

entries.meaning: A tall narrow lab container marked for measuring the volume of a liquid. ---
examples: Measure fifty milliliters in a graduated cylinder.
A graduated cylinder is more accurate than a beaker.
Wash the graduated cylinders after class.

entries.meaning: The unit of power, used for the output of a bulb, speaker, or motor. ---
examples: This bulb uses only nine watts.
The speaker is rated at fifty watts.
A watt is one joule per second.
entries.contrast: In most American speech it sounds just like what.

entries.meaning: One thousand watts. ---
examples: The space heater draws two kilowatts.
The panels produce five kilowatts at noon.
Motors abroad are rated in kilowatts.

entries.meaning: The unit electricity is sold in, equal to one kilowatt used for one hour. ---
examples: We used 800 kilowatt-hours last month.
The rate is twelve cents per kilowatt-hour.
The new panels cut our kilowatt-hours in half.

entries.meaning: The amount of electric power something uses or produces, stated in watts. ---
examples: Check the wattage before you buy the bulb.
Higher wattage means a brighter light.
The microwave's wattage is printed on the back.

entries.meaning: The unit of electrical pressure. ---
examples: American outlets run at 120 volts.
The battery puts out twelve volts.
Nine volts isn't enough for that motor.

entries.meaning: The electrical force in a circuit, measured in volts. ---
examples: Check the voltage before you plug it in.
Low voltage made the lights flicker.
European voltage is twice ours.

entries.meaning: A unit of electric current, short for ampere. ---
examples: That circuit is rated for fifteen amps.
The motor pulls about six amps.
The breaker trips at twenty amps.
entries.contrast: Amp is also short for amplifier, as in a guitar amp.

entries.meaning: The full name of the unit of electric current. ---
examples: The label gives the current in amperes.
One ampere is a lot of current for a thin wire.
Fuses are rated in amperes.
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech almost everyone says amp instead.

entries.meaning: The unit of electrical resistance. ---
examples: The resistor is rated at 100 ohms.
Measure the resistance in ohms.
A few ohms won't matter here.

entries.meaning: A unit of engine power equal to 746 watts. ---
examples: The engine puts out 300 horsepower.
That mower doesn't have much horsepower.
They compared the horsepower of both trucks.
entries.contrast: It stays horsepower after a number, never horsepowers.

entries.meaning: The metric unit of energy or work. ---
examples: The reaction released 500 joules.
One joule is a very small amount of energy.
Convert the calories into joules.
entries.contrast: Pronounced JOOL, exactly like jewel.

entries.meaning: The unit used to measure how loud a sound is. ---
examples: A normal conversation is about sixty decibels.
Hearing damage starts around 85 decibels.
The meter reads in decibels.

entries.meaning: The unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second. ---
examples: American power runs at sixty hertz.
The monitor refreshes at 120 hertz.
People hear sound from about 20 hertz upward.
entries.contrast: The plural is hertz, and the word sounds like hurts.

entries.meaning: The metric unit of force. ---
examples: The spring pulls with a force of ten newtons.
One newton is about the weight of an apple.
Convert the pounds into newtons.
entries.contrast: Americans say NOO-tuhn; the British add a y sound, NYOO-tuhn.

entries.meaning: The turning force produced by an engine or applied to a bolt. ---
examples: Diesel engines make a lot of torque.
Tighten the lug nuts to the right torque.
The wrench measures torque in foot-pounds.
entries.contrast: The que is a plain k sound: TORK.

entries.meaning: The distance between one wave crest and the next. ---
examples: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue.
The antenna is cut to a quarter wavelength.
Only certain wavelengths pass through the filter.

entries.meaning: The unit that measures how much visible light a lamp gives off. ---
examples: This bulb puts out 800 lumens.
Flashlights are rated in lumens now.
A few hundred lumens is plenty for a desk lamp.

entries.meaning: A rating showing how well gasoline resists knocking in an engine. ---
examples: The manual calls for 91 octane.
Higher octane costs more per gallon.
Regular gas is 87 octane in most states.

entries.meaning: The distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees. ---
examples: Chicago sits at about 42 degrees latitude.
Enter the latitude and longitude.
Northern latitudes get very little winter sun.
entries.contrast: Americans say LAT-uh-tood; the British say LAT-i-tyood.

entries.meaning: The distance east or west of the prime meridian, measured in degrees. ---
examples: The ship radioed in its longitude.
Lines of longitude meet at the poles.
Two cities at the same longitude can have very different weather.
entries.contrast: The g is a j sound: LAHN-juh-tood.

entries.meaning: Height above sea level. ---
examples: Denver sits at an elevation of about a mile.
The trail gains 2,000 feet of elevation.
Water boils sooner at high elevations.

entries.meaning: The average level of the ocean's surface, used as the zero point for heights. ---
examples: The town is 300 feet above sea level.
Sea level has risen several inches in a century.
Baking times change well above sea level.

entries.meaning: The space between two lines that meet, measured in degrees. ---
examples: Cut the trim at a 45-degree angle.
Measure the angle with a protractor.
All three angles add up to 180 degrees.

entries.meaning: One of a set of numbers giving an exact position. ---
examples: Send me the coordinates and I'll find it.
Each coordinate is given in degrees.
The GPS coordinates were off by a block.
entries.contrast: The noun ends in -nut; the verb to coordinate ends in -nayt.

entries.meaning: One long step, or the distance covered by it. ---
examples: He crossed the room in three strides.
The runner's stride got shorter near the end.
Long strides eat up the distance.

entries.meaning: The inside diameter of a gun barrel. ---
examples: The rifle is a .22 caliber.
Police recovered a bullet of the same caliber.
The shop stocks several calibers.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it caliber; the British write calibre.

entries.meaning: The hollow inside of a tube or a gun barrel, or the width of it. ---
examples: The engine has a four-inch bore.
Clean the bore after every trip to the range.
The two cylinders have identical bores.
entries.contrast: Sounds the same as boar, a wild pig, and as bore, the past tense of bear.

entries.meaning: A single item or amount taken for testing or study. ---
examples: The lab needs a urine specimen.
Each specimen is labeled and dated.
Museum specimens are kept behind glass.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable: SPES-uh-muhn.

entries.meaning: The weight of the contents alone, without the packaging. ---
examples: The net weight is printed on the side of the box.
The net weight is twelve ounces.
Compare the net weights, not the package sizes.

entries.meaning: The changing of a measurement from one unit into another.
examples: The chart gives the conversion from inches to centimeters.
Do the conversion before you order the parts.
Unit conversions trip up a lot of students.
